title: Post-influenza secondary pneumonia: Staphylococcus aureus
vignette: A 54-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to worsening fever, cough, and shortness of breath. The patient initially presented a week ago with a fever, headache, myalgia, nasal discharge, and a sore throat. He tested positive for influenza A and was discharged home with symptomatic treatment. The patient's symptoms gradually improved, but over the past 2 days he has had high fevers, cough productive of yellowish sputum, sharp right-sided chest pain, and shortness of breath. The patient has no other medical problems and does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Temperature is 38.9 C (102 F), blood pressure is 118/66 mm Hg, and pulse is 110/min. Physical examination reveals right-sided lung crackles. Chest x-ray reveals infiltrates in the right lung. Which of the following pathogens is most likely to be isolated from this patient's sputum?

clues.note: Influenza damages the respiratory epithelium (loss of cilia) and predisposes to SECONDARY bacterial pneumonia in the following days.

clues.text: symptoms gradually improved, but over the past 2 days he has had high fevers
clues.note: A biphasic course - influenza improving, then WORSENING with high fever and productive cough - is the classic signal of post-influenza secondary bacterial pneumonia.
Purulent sputum plus focal infiltrate indicates a bacterial pneumonia (consolidation), not ongoing viral illness.
Focal crackles with a lobar infiltrate confirm bacterial consolidation.

whatMatters: An improving influenza illness that then WORSENS with high fever, purulent sputum, and a focal infiltrate = post-influenza secondary bacterial pneumonia. The leading pathogens are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae; of the listed choices, Staphylococcus aureus is the classic post-influenza organism (especially in young, previously healthy patients). Answer E.
strategy: Recognize the biphasic 'flu then worse' pattern -> secondary bacterial pneumonia, then pick the best-fitting listed organism: S. aureus (E) is the classic post-influenza pathogen. Eliminate CMV (immunocompromised, interstitial), Klebsiella (alcoholic/aspiration, currant-jelly sputum), Listeria (neonates/immunocompromised, not pneumonia), and nontuberculous mycobacteria (AIDS/chronic, not acute post-flu).

eliminations.label: Cytomegalovirus - immunocompromised, interstitial
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: CMV pneumonia occurs in immunocompromised hosts (AIDS, transplant) with bilateral interstitial infiltrates. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is not associated with post-influenza pneumonia in an immunocompetent patient with a focal infiltrate. ✅ Correct if: interstitial pneumonia in an immunocompromised patient.

eliminations.label: Klebsiella pneumoniae - alcoholic/aspiration
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: Klebsiella causes nosocomial/aspiration pneumonia with thick, blood-tinged 'currant-jelly' sputum in alcoholics or debilitated patients. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is not the typical post-influenza organism. ✅ Correct if: an alcoholic with currant-jelly sputum and cavitary/necrotizing pneumonia.

eliminations.label: Listeria monocytogenes - not a pneumonia bug
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: Listeria causes meningitis/sepsis in neonates, the elderly, pregnant women, and the immunocompromised. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it doesn't cause typical community pneumonia. ✅ Correct if: neonatal or immunocompromised meningitis/sepsis.

eliminations.label: Nontuberculous mycobacteria - chronic/AIDS
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: NTM (e.g., MAC) causes chronic pulmonary disease or disseminated infection in AIDS. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it's a chronic, not acute post-influenza, process. ✅ Correct if: chronic cough in AIDS or structural lung disease.

reasoning: Influenza injures the respiratory epithelium (loss of cilia), predisposing to secondary bacterial pneumonia
The course is biphasic: flu improves, then worsens with high fever, purulent sputum, and a focal infiltrate
Leading post-influenza pathogens: S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, H. influenzae
-> of the choices, Staphylococcus aureus; answer E
mechanism: Influenza virus attacks the tracheobronchial epithelium and causes loss of cilia, impairing mucociliary clearance and promoting bacterial colonization; viral neuraminidase also exposes host cell-surface sugars that foster bacterial adherence. This predisposes recovering patients to SECONDARY bacterial pneumonia, classically heralded by a biphasic course - initial improvement followed by worsening fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, and a focal infiltrate. The leading organisms are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae; although the elderly are most often affected overall, post-influenza S. aureus pneumonia characteristically develops in young, previously healthy patients and can be severe/necrotizing. The distractors fit other settings (CMV - immunocompromised/interstitial; Klebsiella - alcoholic/aspiration currant-jelly sputum; Listeria - neonatal/immunocompromised; NTM - chronic/AIDS).
